tracks.title: The grammar of the ecosystem
tracks.text: Lesson four — org. Org is the grammar of the ecosystem. Plain text that holds prose, tasks, dates, and runnable code… in one parseable tree. People write it. Agents write it. Machines can test it. [curious] This lesson explains why that one trick holds everything else together.

tracks.title: The missing layer
tracks.text: Every serious project has a second product nobody ships. The intent. Why this exists… what's done… what's next… what we decided — and when. Today, that layer is scattered. A README that's half true. Tickets in one silo… the spec in another… and the agent's context in none of them. [sighs] And the formats on offer force a bad trade. Markdown is lovely to read, and means nothing to a machine. It's a blogging language. You can't validate it… you can't test it… you can't reliably parse a plan out of it. And YAML and JSON fail the opposite way. They parse perfectly… and can't hold a paragraph of reasoning. Prose, or structure — pick one. [excited] The ecosystem refuses to pick.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Org is the ecosystem's written layer. Plain text that holds prose, tasks, dates, and runnable code, in one parseable tree. Readable by people… writable by agents… testable by machines. The name comes from org-mode — the format it grew from. And in Workbooks, org is simply the grammar everything is authored in. The same way the web settled on HTML for what things look like… the ecosystem settles on org for what things mean.

tracks.title: Born twenty years early
tracks.text: Org-mode appeared in the Emacs world around two thousand three — as a way to keep notes, to-dos, and schedules in plain text. It sits in the lineage of literate programming. Donald Knuth's old, stubborn idea… that code should live inside the explanation of why it exists. Not the other way around. And over two decades, it quietly grew the exact feature set agent systems are now reinventing — badly. Task states. Timestamps. Dependencies. And tangling… source code written inside the document, extractable to real files. [excited] And here's the accident of history that makes it perfect now. Those twenty years of documentation are in every model's training data. Agents don't have to be taught org. They arrived knowing it.

tracks.title: What one file can hold
tracks.text: [curious] What can one file hold? Four things. First — headlines. A real hierarchy… sections machines can navigate. Second — prose. The reasoning, in full sentences, where it belongs. Third — tasks and dates. To-do states, schedules, deadlines… native, not convention. And fourth — code blocks. Runnable source in any language, tangled out to real files. Here's a taste of what that looks like. A real deployment, described entirely in org. A headline that says where the engine runs. A database choice. A scheduled task to rotate a signing key. And a paragraph of plain reasoning about why it's single-tenant… for now. Configuration, a schedule, and intent. One file… [excited] and every line of it is parseable.

tracks.title: Why not just Markdown?
tracks.text: [curious] Why not just Markdown? Use Markdown! It's wonderful — for writing. The trouble starts when you ask it to run a system. There are no states… no dates… no dependencies. Just headings… [chuckles] and vibes. When an agent drifts — writes one file too many, contradicts itself across notes — Markdown has no way to even notice. You can't write a test suite for Markdown. You can, for org. Parse the tree… check the states… validate the dates… diff the intent. And that's the whole argument, in one line. Markdown is for telling humans things. [excited] Org is for telling humans and systems the same thing… at once.

tracks.title: Where it shows up
tracks.text: [curious] Where does org show up? Five places. First — inside every workbook. It's the writable layer where intent, tasks, and memory live. Second — toolkit manuals. The readable surface that doubles as the tool's interface. Third — deployments. One declarative org file describes the whole engine setup. Fourth — workflows. Plans whose tasks and dependencies render straight to boards and timelines. And fifth — agent definitions. Who an agent is… written in the same grammar it works in. [excited] One grammar everywhere is the quiet superpower. Every piece of the ecosystem can read every other piece… and so can you.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Honesty section. Plain text drifts. Agents writing freely will eventually write too much… or twice… or contradictorily. Org doesn't prevent that. No format does. What it does, is make drift detectable. Because the layer is parseable, a checker — or another agent — can walk the tree and find the contradiction. And org is not a database. Heavy structured data belongs in the workbook's SQLite… not in headlines. Use each layer for what it's for.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I have to learn Emacs? [chuckles] No. Org the format left Emacs the editor behind long ago. Any text editor works — and most org here is written by tools and agents anyway. Your job is mostly to read it… which takes about four minutes to learn. Will I be writing org by hand all day? Rarely. You write prose and intentions… the toolchain keeps the structure. Think of it like git — you don't hand-edit the object store either. Should my README be org now? Keep READMEs in Markdown — that's its home turf. Org earns its keep where systems need to read what you wrote. And — is this a proprietary format? The opposite. A twenty-year-old open convention, with parsers in every language. Workbooks adopts it precisely because it belongs to nobody.

tracks.title: Wrapping up
tracks.text: So that's org. One grammar — prose and structure in the same file. Readable by you… writable by agents… testable by machines. [curious] And now that you have the grammar… let's meet who's writing in it. The agents. Agents.
